item.title: Example-Driven Refactoring Tames Complexity By Reducing Choices
item.dc:creator: Jamie Rivera
item.content:encoded:
When I joined the example project three years ago I inherited a small internal tool called Zorp. It had grown from a weekend script into something the whole team depended on, and nobody was quite sure anymore which parts were load-bearing.

The first week I spent just reading. I renamed a few variables, split one enormous function into three smaller ones, and ran the existing example test suite after every change. Nothing broke, so I kept going.

A Structural Habit

What I settled into was a habit: before changing behavior, change only the shape of the code. Extract a function. Rename a value. Inline a wrapper that no longer wrapped anything useful. Each step was small enough that if the example test suite failed, I knew exactly which change to undo.

Over a few months, Zorp's structure slowly became legible. Modules that used to reach across the whole codebase now depended on a handful of narrow interfaces. None of this was visible from the outside; the tool behaved exactly the same on day ninety as it had on day one.

Why It Mattered

The payoff came later, when a genuinely new feature was requested. Because Zorp's internals were now organized around clear seams, the feature fit into a single module instead of touching a dozen files. What would have been a risky, multi-week change became a contained, one-day addition.

I don't think this habit is exotic. It's closer to gardening than engineering: small, frequent, reversible adjustments that keep a system tidy enough that bigger changes stay possible. The example of Zorp is fictional, but the habit is one I'd recommend to anyone maintaining a system that has quietly become load-bearing.

item.title: Tune Your Example Workflow For Rate Of Change
item.dc:creator: Jamie Rivera
item.content:encoded:
This is a second fictional example post used only to verify that the feed parser can handle multiple items in a single author feed. It contains no real content and describes no real event.

The fictional Zorp platform mentioned in this feed is a placeholder used purely for testing the extraction of article bodies from syndicated feeds.
